name: Venezuelan waltz

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: An articulate dance historian and musicologist passionate about South American partner forms and cross-rhythmic adaptations.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Listen for the Piano, Classical guitar, Violin, Bandola.
The pulse is 3/4.

Characterized by an eight-measure broken melody that plays with silences and off-beat accents over standard three-quarter time. Salon versions feature solo piano or classical guitar, while regional popular versions use bright lead violins or bandolas anchored by rhythmic strumming on the cuatro and guitar.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Venezuelan waltz is influence of Joropo: The Venezuelan waltz served as a foundational musical and dance base for the joropo.
Venezuelan waltz is influence of Tamunangue: Waltz forms and rhythms are integrated into traditional folk suites like the tamunangue.
Venezuelan waltz is variant of Pasillo: An Andean adaptation of the Venezuelan waltz cultivated in western high regions and adjacent Colombian territories.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.rhythm_pattern: Syncopated 3/4 with off-beat silences breaking European metric symmetry
music_brief.vocal_style: Romantic lyric singing in vals-canción and vals pasaje forms
music_brief.musical_form: Two-part structure in salon waltzes; three-part structure in popular oral tradition waltzes; 8-bar melodic phrasing
music_brief.sound_description: Characterized by an eight-measure broken melody that plays with silences and off-beat accents over standard three-quarter time. Salon versions feature solo piano or classical guitar, while regional popular versions use bright lead violins or bandolas anchored by rhythmic strumming on the cuatro and guitar.
listen_before_composing: Dama antañona — Francisco de Paula Aguirre
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Venezuelan waltz (Venezuela). Meter 3/4. Rhythm pattern: Syncopated 3/4 with off-beat silences breaking European metric symmetry. Instruments: Piano, Classical guitar, Violin, Bandola, Cuatro, Tiple, Mandolin. Vocal style: Romantic lyric singing in vals-canción and vals pasaje forms. Form: Two-part structure in salon waltzes; three-part structure in popular oral tradition waltzes; 8-bar melodic phrasing. Mood: Lyrical, Romantic, Syncopated, Playful, Dramatic. It should sound like this: Characterized by an eight-measure broken melody that plays with silences and off-beat accents over standard three-quarter time. Salon versions feature solo piano or classical guitar, while regional popular versions use bright lead violins or bandolas anchored by rhythmic strumming on the cuatro and guitar. New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.

wardrobe.policy: neutral dress: the sources do not describe the costume yet
care: every element traceable to the costume notes or a licensed image; nothing added for effect
no caricature, no exaggeration, no mixing of regions or eras
a culture bearer reviews the wardrobe before production; the review is recorded in the pack
credits name the tradition and the sources of the reconstruction
